newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan awaits US envoy amid signs of trade friction.
newsitem.headline: Japan awaits US envoy amid signs of trade friction.

text.p: Japanese hoping for a word on who will become the next U.S. envoy to Tokyo got a clue -- but no confirmation -- on Tuesday, when former House Speaker Tom Foley failed to attend a news conference by a wise-men group.
But signs are growing that whoever assumes the post will face some tough times ahead on the U.S.-Japan trade front.

Foley, reported in April by U.S. media to be a virtual shoo-in for the ambassador's post, was scheduled to attend but did not take part in a two-day meeting of a U.S.-Japan wise-men's group and a closing news conference on Tuesday.
"I have a very clear understanding of why Mr Foley is not here, but I'm not at liberty to talk about it," former U.S. Trade Representative William Brock told the news conference.

Rumours that the 68-year old Foley would be nominated as U.S. ambassador to Japan have swirled ever since Walter Mondale resigned the post last December, ending a three-year term marked by trade feuds and frayed security ties.
Brock said many U.S. diplomatic appointments had been delayed by "competing pressures" on President Bill Clinton's administration, including talks on a balanced budget agreement.
"The truth of the matter is that our appointment process has been waxing exceedingly slow in a number of areas," Brock said, adding that quick action was now expected on key posts.
"My expectation is you will see some very quick action regarding Japan. I can't tell you who or when, but I think you know who and I think it will be soon," he said.
The vacancy in the ambassadorial post coincides with signs of potential turbulence in U.S.-Japan trade ties.

"In our view, we are entering a rather delicate and potentially difficult period in U.S.-Japan trade relations," a U.S. official told reporters on Tuesday, noting concerns about signs that Japan's trade surplus might be on the rise again and that fiscal tightening could quash its economic recovery.
"It's like a drought in the forest -- it doesn't take much of a spark to create a fire," the U.S. official said.

Japanese have already warmly welcomed the expected appointment of Foley -- whom they view as a heavy-weight politician who understands Japan. "He knows Japan well and he is very influential," said one Japanese businessman.
Some U.S. critics, however, have opposed Foley's nomination on the grounds that he might be too soft on Tokyo in trade feuds and not fight hard enough for U.S. business interests.

The silver-haired Democrat was a member of the House from Washington State for 30 years from 1965 until he lost a re-election bid in 1994. He served as Speaker, the highest post in the House of Representatives, from 1989 to 1994 and is currently with a top U.S. law firm.
